title: Dexcom G6's “Urgent Low Soon” predictive alert may cut time below 54 mg/dL, by less in controlled trials
summary: Dexcom's analyses of 1,424 and 15,000 users link the G6's 20-minute Urgent Low Soon alert to less hypoglycemia; authors of an independent trial in 24 adults found a reduction only below 2.8 mmol/L.
account: The Dexcom G6 continuous glucose monitor was classified by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) under De Novo DEN170088 on 27 March 2018. Its “Urgent Low Soon” (ULS) alert fires when an algorithm predicts an estimated glucose value of 55 mg/dL or below within 20 minutes. The FDA decision summary describes the threshold and predictive alerts as intended to warn patients to act before a hypoglycemic event. Dexcom employees Puhr, Derdzinski, Welsh, Parker, Walker and Price compared 1,424 users before and after they moved from the G5 (no predictive alert) to the G6 between 1 May and 31 August 2018. Their anonymized comparison was in Diabetes Technology & Therapeutics (online 22 March 2019). With a 70 mg/dL low-threshold setting (n=658), time below 54 mg/dL fell from 1.0% to 0.6%. With an 80 mg/dL setting (n=766), it fell from 0.6% to 0.4% (both P<0.001). ULS fired 0.9 and 0.6 times a day. A second Dexcom analysis (Puhr et al., Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology, online 3 April 2019; abstract only) had 15,000 G6 app users. More than 93% had ULS enabled. Its use was associated with less time below 55 and 70 mg/dL regardless of how often users viewed the app. Clinicians at six Belgian hospitals ran the Dexcom-funded ALERTT1 trial and reported on 2 June 2021 that 3 of 127 adults on the G6 had severe hypoglycemia over six months, against 13 of 127 on FreeStyle Libre. They compared whole systems, so the result does not isolate the alert. In 2022 Dexcom staff reported that hypoglycemia also fell after the switch in Germany, Sweden and the United Kingdom. ULS use dropped from 96% to 98% of users to 84% to 87%, and the authors could not test whether the alert itself made the difference. Independent evidence is thinner. The PACE crossover randomized trial at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust had 24 adults with type 1 diabetes. Each had ULS on or off for 40 days. Its authors found no difference in hypoglycemia below 3.0 or 3.9 mmol/L in the 24 hours after exercise. Time below 2.8 mmol/L was lower with ULS on (P=0.04). In 2024 researchers in Ulm argued that outside checks of predictive alerts are hard because the algorithms are proprietary. Preechasuk et al. (Imperial College London) had 29 adults who switched from FreeStyle Libre 2 to a Dexcom G7 with ULS. They spent less time below 70 mg/dL (3.0% to 2.0%, P=0.006). That design changes the device and the alert together. Clinicians in Prague later reported a patient with impaired hypoglycemia awareness whose continuous glucose monitor with ULS on did not eliminate prolonged hypoglycemia. He sometimes muted the alerts. None of the sources calls the predictive algorithm machine learning.
purpose: Built to warn users 20 minutes before predicted serious hypoglycemia so they can act. The reported reductions in time below 54–55 mg/dL are that purpose.

ai_role.statement: The alert is generated when the G6 algorithm forecasts glucose at or below 55 mg/dL within 20 minutes. Users still have to act on it. The principal outcome evidence is the maker's own real-world analyses (Puhr et al. 2019, 2020). They compare the same users before and after the G6 transition without a control arm. The independent Imperial College PACE randomized trial found no difference at 3.0 or 3.9 mmol/L after exercise and a difference only below 2.8 mmol/L. The Imperial switch study cannot separate the alert from the change of device. None of the sources describes the prediction method as machine learning.

evidence.citation: Acciaroli G, van der Linden J, Chao C, Walker TC, Oliver N. Longitudinal analysis of users transitioning from the Dexcom G5 to the G6 RT-CGM system in Germany, Sweden and the United Kingdom (2018-2020). Diabetic Medicine 40(2):e14946, online 8 September 2022. Four authors are Dexcom employees and the fifth has received Dexcom funding; they report that hypoglycemia fell after the switch to the G6 in all three countries, and they state that they could not test whether turning the ULS alert on or off changed outcomes.
evidence.title: Longitudinal analysis of users transitioning from the Dexcom G5 to the G6 RT-CGM system in Germany, Sweden and the United Kingdom (2018-2020)
evidence.quote: In all three countries, the transition from G5 to G6 was associated with a clear decrease in hypoglycaemia.

evidence.citation: Visser MM, Charleer S, Fieuws S, et al. Comparing real-time and intermittently scanned continuous glucose monitoring in adults with type 1 diabetes (ALERTT1): a 6-month, prospective, multicentre, randomised controlled trial. The Lancet 397(10291):2275-2283, online 2 June 2021. Clinicians at six Belgian hospitals ran the trial with Dexcom funding. They report that adults randomized to the Dexcom G6 had less hypoglycemia than adults kept on FreeStyle Libre, but they compared whole systems, so the predictive alert cannot be isolated.
evidence.title: Comparing real-time and intermittently scanned continuous glucose monitoring in adults with type 1 diabetes (ALERTT1): a 6-month, prospective, multicentre, randomised controlled trial
evidence.quote: Fewer participants on rtCGM experienced severe hypoglycaemia (n=3 vs n=13; p=0·0082).

evidence.citation: Pleus S, Eichenlaub M, Waldenmaier D, Freckmann G. A Critical Discussion of Alert Evaluations in the Context of Continuous Glucose Monitoring System Performance. Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology 18(4):847-856, online 13 March 2024. The authors work at the Institute for Diabetes Technology in Ulm, which has received research support and fees from Dexcom and other makers. Their review covers CGM alerts in general, and they argue that predictive alerts are hard to check because the prediction algorithms are proprietary.
evidence.title: A Critical Discussion of Alert Evaluations in the Context of Continuous Glucose Monitoring System Performance
evidence.quote: For predictive alerts, fewer results were found in the literature, and retrospective determination of CGM alert timing is complicated by the prediction algorithms being proprietary information.

fields.account: The Dexcom G6 continuous glucose monitor was classified by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) under De Novo DEN170088 on 27 March 2018. Its “Urgent Low Soon” (ULS) alert fires when an algorithm predicts an estimated glucose value of 55 mg/dL or below within 20 minutes. The FDA decision summary describes the threshold and predictive alerts as intended to warn patients to act before a hypoglycemic event. Dexcom employees Puhr, Derdzinski, Welsh, Parker, Walker and Price compared 1,424 users before and after they moved from the G5 (no predictive alert) to the G6 between 1 May and 31 August 2018. Their anonymized comparison was in Diabetes Technology & Therapeutics (online 22 March 2019). With a 70 mg/dL low-threshold setting (n=658), time below 54 mg/dL fell from 1.0% to 0.6%. With an 80 mg/dL setting (n=766), it fell from 0.6% to 0.4% (both P<0.001). ULS fired 0.9 and 0.6 times a day. A second Dexcom analysis (Puhr et al., Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology, online 3 April 2019; abstract only) had 15,000 G6 app users. More than 93% had ULS enabled. Its use was associated with less time below 55 and 70 mg/dL regardless of how often users viewed the app. Clinicians at six Belgian hospitals ran the Dexcom-funded ALERTT1 trial and reported on 2 June 2021 that 3 of 127 adults on the G6 had severe hypoglycemia over six months, against 13 of 127 on FreeStyle Libre. They compared whole systems, so the result does not isolate the alert. In 2022 Dexcom staff reported that hypoglycemia also fell after the switch in Germany, Sweden and the United Kingdom. ULS use dropped from 96% to 98% of users to 84% to 87%, and the authors could not test whether the alert itself made the difference. Independent evidence is thinner. The PACE crossover randomized trial at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust had 24 adults with type 1 diabetes. Each had ULS on or off for 40 days. Its authors found no difference in hypoglycemia below 3.0 or 3.9 mmol/L in the 24 hours after exercise. Time below 2.8 mmol/L was lower with ULS on (P=0.04). In 2024 researchers in Ulm argued that outside checks of predictive alerts are hard because the algorithms are proprietary. Preechasuk et al. (Imperial College London) had 29 adults who switched from FreeStyle Libre 2 to a Dexcom G7 with ULS. They spent less time below 70 mg/dL (3.0% to 2.0%, P=0.006). That design changes the device and the alert together. Clinicians in Prague later reported a patient with impaired hypoglycemia awareness whose continuous glucose monitor with ULS on did not eliminate prolonged hypoglycemia. He sometimes muted the alerts. None of the sources calls the predictive algorithm machine learning.

Its “Urgent Low Soon” (ULS) alert fires when an algorithm predicts an estimated glucose value of 55 mg/dL or below within 20 minutes. The FDA decision summary describes the threshold and predictive alerts as intended to warn patients to act before a hypoglycemic event. Dexcom employees Puhr, Derdzinski, Welsh, Parker, Walker and Price compared 1,424 users before and after they moved from the G5 (no predictive alert) to the G6 between 1 May and 31 August 2018. Their anonymized comparison was in Diabetes Technology & Therapeutics (online 22 March 2019). With a 70 mg/dL low-threshold setting (n=658), time below 54 mg/dL fell from 1.0% to 0.6%. With an 80 mg/dL setting (n=766), it fell from 0.6% to 0.4% (both P<0.001). ULS fired 0.9 and 0.6 times a day. A second Dexcom analysis (Puhr et al., Journal of Diabetes Science and Technology, online 3 April 2019; abstract only) had 15,000 G6 app users. More than 93% had ULS enabled. Its use was associated with less time below 55 and 70 mg/dL regardless of how often users viewed the app. Clinicians at six Belgian hospitals ran the Dexcom-funded ALERTT1 trial and reported on 2 June 2021 that 3 of 127 adults on the G6 had severe hypoglycemia over six months, against 13 of 127 on FreeStyle Libre. They compared whole systems, so the result does not isolate the alert. In 2022 Dexcom staff reported that hypoglycemia also fell after the switch in Germany, Sweden and the United Kingdom. ULS use dropped from 96% to 98% of users to 84% to 87%, and the authors could not test whether the alert itself made the difference. Independent evidence is thinner. The PACE crossover randomized trial at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust had 24 adults with type 1 diabetes. Each had ULS on or off for 40 days. Its authors found no difference in hypoglycemia below 3.0 or 3.9 mmol/L in the 24 hours after exercise. Time below 2.8 mmol/L was lower with ULS on (P=0.04). In 2024 researchers in Ulm argued that outside checks of predictive alerts are hard because the algorithms are proprietary. Preechasuk et al. (Imperial College London) had 29 adults who switched from FreeStyle Libre 2 to a Dexcom G7 with ULS. They spent less time below 70 mg/dL (3.0% to 2.0%, P=0.006). That design changes the device and the alert together. Clinicians in Prague later reported a patient with impaired hypoglycemia awareness whose continuous glucose monitor with ULS on did not eliminate prolonged hypoglycemia. He sometimes muted the alerts. None of the sources calls the predictive algorithm machine learning.

produced_by: Real-time CGM with the ULS alert enabled (over 93% of G6 app users in Dexcom's sample)
Users who respond to the alert by treating or adjusting insulin, which the sources assume rather than measure
A low-threshold alert also set (70 or 80 mg/dL in the Dexcom analysis)
must_hold: Users keep the alert on rather than muting it for alarm fatigue, as the Prague patient sometimes did
Sensor accuracy sufficient to avoid nuisance alerts, which Puhr et al. cite as a cause of CGM discontinuation
Benefit beyond a plain threshold alert, which the PACE trial found only below 2.8 mmol/L
